New York City Council: local ideal points, 2014–2026

Pooled stated-meeting roll calls · Preliminary analysis

Published

September 18, 2026

This analysis places every member of the New York City Council who cast a recorded vote between November 2014 and September 2026 on one voting scale — 123 people across four council classes. The plots show the council seated in January 2026; their coordinates come from the pooled fit, so they remain comparable with the earlier members who are not drawn.

The recovered dimension separates the council’s Republicans from its Democrats completely, tracks caucus membership and DSA endorsements, and is strongly associated with how each district voted for president in 2024, for council in 2023 and 2025, and for mayor in 2025.

Dataset

The roll calls come from the MyTown corpus of local-government meetings and votes (Jacob Greene, 2026, CC BY 4.0, DOI 10.57967/hf/9676), release of September 18, 2026. Preserved local extracts, rather than later downloads, define this analysis.

Coverage and construction

Measure Value
Member-vote records 293,979
Stated meetings 207
Coverage November 13, 2014 – September 10, 2026
People 123
Meeting–motion items 5,842
Items with at least two members per side 746
Items retained for the fit 737
Usable yea/nay votes 34,773
Members of the council seated January 2026 52

Each meeting–motion combination is one vote event. Yea is coded 1 and nay 0. Every other recorded status — absence, abstention, medical, maternity, paternity, bereavement, suspension — is missing, never a nay. An item is retained when at least two members voted on each side and at least 40 members voted at all, which leaves 737 contested roll calls. Most stated-meeting business is unanimous, so this is a small and deliberately selected slice of what the council does.

Fifty-two people appear in the current council because Erik Bottcher voted at the January 15, 2026 meeting before leaving the seat now held by another member.

Results

The council seated in January 2026

An ideal point is a one-dimensional summary of voting similarity: members near one another take the same side on contested roll calls, and members far apart oppose one another. The units are specific to this New York sample and cannot be compared numerically with the Chicago, Denver, or Houston scores.

The current council runs from Tiffany Cabán (-1.66) and Alexa Avilés (-1.63) at one end to Vickie Paladino (2.48), Inna Vernikov (2.18), David Carr (2.18) and Joann Ariola (2.17) at the other. Most Democrats sit in a crowded middle whose intervals overlap heavily; the ordering within that middle should not be read as a ranking.

Across the full twelve years the extremes are wider still: Jumaane Williams (-4.50) and Charles Barron (-2.93) at one end, Steven Matteo (3.34) and Joseph Borelli (3.19) at the other. Two placements deserve caution: Vincent Ignizio (2.58) rests on 5 retained votes, and Williams, the most extreme estimate in the analysis, on 116.

The earlier councils

Each council below is drawn on the same axis, so positions can be compared across classes. Coordinates come from the single pooled fit rather than from separate models.

Council Members Contested items voted
2014-2017 56 1170

2022-2023 51 1100
2024-2025 54 1093

The 2018–2021 council contributes by far the most contested votes; the council seated in 2026 has only eight months of record so far, which is why its intervals are wider than its size alone would suggest.

Party and organizational groupings

These labels are external evidence assembled from official rosters, Board of Elections results, and organizational announcements. None of them enters the model, the starting values, or the orientation of the scale.

Group Scope In group Mean: group Mean: others Pairs ordered as expected
Official council party: Republican current council 5 2.15 -0.27 100%
Won on a Republican ballot line (2017-2025) all 123 11 2.06 -0.20 99%
Common-Sense Caucus (ever) all 123 16 1.36 -0.20 93%
Progressive Caucus (ever) all 123 61 -0.43 0.43 77%
DSA campaign endorsement (ever) all 123 2 -1.65 0.03 98%
DSA officeholder bloc (ever) all 123 4 -1.41 0.05 97%
Also served in the state legislature all 123 16 0.11 -0.02 55%

The council’s five Republicans are the five most positive members of the current council, with no overlap at all: every Republican–Democrat pair is ordered as expected. Members who ever won on a Republican ballot line average 2.06 against -0.20. The Common-Sense Caucus sits toward that end even though it has always included Democrats, and the Progressive Caucus and both DSA measures sit at the other. Service in the state legislature shows almost no separation, which is the right result: it is a biographical fact, not an ideological one, and it works as a bridge to state-level scales precisely because it is not itself a measure of position.

District electorates

Every council election, 2017 to 2025

The same comparison repeats for each election that seated one of these councils: the Republican-line share of a district’s council vote against the position of the member it elected. The association is present in every cycle (Pearson 0.64 to 0.76).

  • 2025

Election Districts Pearson Spearman
2017 50 0.64 0.35

One 2017 winner never cast a retained vote and so has no coordinate, leaving 50 districts that year.

All four comparisons

Comparison Districts Pearson Spearman
2024 presidential vote (Trump two-party share) 51 0.72 0.55
2023 council election (Republican-line share) 51 0.76 0.44
2025 council election (Republican-line share) 51 0.71 0.34
2025 mayoral vote (Mamdani share of top three) 51 -0.75 -0.68

Trump’s two-party share correlates 0.72 with council position across all 51 districts — a ten-point increase corresponds to 0.38 ideal-point units (R² = 0.52). The council’s own elections give the same picture from a different ballot. The mayoral comparison runs the other way by construction: districts where Mamdani polled better elected more progressive members (-0.75).

The mayoral figures come from the Board of Elections election-district files, aggregated to all 51 council districts using the same election’s council result files as the crosswalk — all 4,117 in-play election districts match exactly one district. The presidential figures aggregate the New York Times published precinct polygons to the council boundaries. BOE 2025 results; New York Times precinct data

Interpretation and limits

A single dimension estimated from twelve years of contested stated-meeting votes reproduces the council’s party division exactly, its organized caucuses closely, and the partisan geography of its districts in four consecutive elections. That is a strong result for a body whose recorded divisions are rare.

How far the estimates can be pushed — what pooling assumes, how thinly the eras are connected, and which placements rest on very few votes — is set out in the technical appendix.
